docs.title: Chevron
docs.text:
Chevron is a modern Python implementation of Mustache. It is a maintained fork of the original chevron, with current Python support, pinned Mustache conformance fixtures, safe opt-in filesystem partials, explicit lambda protocols, and optional AnyIO-based asynchronous rendering.

Start with Getting started for a complete, small application example. The template-language guide explains what template authors can write; the API reference describes how an application supplies templates, data, partials, and diagnostics.

docs.title: Choose the right entry point
docs.text:
• Use render() for ordinary synchronous Python applications.
  • Use async_render() inside an existing AnyIO runtime when template readers, iterables, or lambdas may await I/O.
  • Use chevron.tokenizer.tokenize() when an application owns template compilation or caching and wants to reuse a validated token stream.

Chevron follows the upstream Mustache manual for the language, then documents its supported extensions and compatibility details separately.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Chevron requires Python 3.11 or later. The core package renders synchronously. Async rendering additionally needs the anyio extra; applications that run on Trio also need the trio extra.

The following example renders a useful page fragment rather than a single replacement. The template can stay with the application, while the view data is a normal Python mapping.

import chevron

template = """<article>
  <h1>{{title}}</h1>
  {{#summary}}<p>{{summary}}</p>{{/summary}}
  <ul>{{#tags}}<li>{{.}}</li>{{/tags}}</ul>
</article>"""

page = chevron.render(
    template,
    {
        "title": "Release notes",
        "summary": "Changes ready for review.",
        "tags": ["documentation", "mustache"],
    },
)

The result is one complete string. Values are HTML-escaped by default, sections repeat or omit content according to their value, and {{.}} means the current list item. Continue with values and contexts for those rules.

docs.title: A useful division of responsibility
docs.text:
Templates decide presentation. Application code decides which data, partial mappings, filesystem directory, lambda mapping, and logger are safe to expose. Chevron does not turn a template into a sandbox: do not place secrets or powerful application objects in template data merely because a template is untrusted.

For an application that keeps reusable components in memory, pass partials_dict; for a controlled template directory, pass partials_path. The partials and layouts chapter covers both patterns.

docs.title: async_render()
docs.text:
await chevron.async_render(template="", data={}, ..., logger=None, log_level=logging.WARNING)

async_render() has the same arguments and rendering semantics as render(), but it may await template readers, iterable values, and declared lambdas. It is available only with the optional AnyIO support and must be called from an existing AnyIO-compatible runtime. Chevron never creates or chooses an event loop for you.

import chevron


async def render_dashboard() -> str:
    return await chevron.async_render(
        "{{#jobs}}{{> job}}{{/jobs}}",
        {"jobs": await load_jobs()},
        partials_dict={"job": "<li>{{name}}: {{status}}</li>\n"},
    )

docs.title: Awaitable values and readers
docs.text:
Declared interpolation and section lambdas may return an ordinary result or an awaitable. Async template readers may implement an async read() method, and values may be asynchronous iterables. A synchronous reader is adapted only where necessary because regular Python file objects do not have portable native async reads.

Do not perform blocking application I/O directly in a callback. Use the application runtime or AnyIO explicitly, for example await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(blocking_function). Chevron does not move application callbacks to workers because doing so would alter their thread affinity and context.

docs.title: Compatibility callbacks
docs.text:
An @chevron.compat callback receives (body, render). Under async_render(), render is always an asynchronous callable: calling it returns an awaitable string. This is true even if the compatibility callback itself is a normal synchronous def.

A synchronous callback may forward that awaitable unchanged, allowing Chevron to await it:

@chevron.compat
def forward(body: str, render):
    return render(body, {"name": "Ada"})


result = await chevron.async_render(
    "{{#forward}}Hello {{name}}{{/forward}}",
    lambdas={"forward": forward},
)
# "Hello Ada"

It cannot inspect or transform the nested string because it has no async context in which to await it. Use async def whenever the callback needs that result:

@chevron.compat
async def emphasize(body: str, render) -> str:
    nested = await render(body, {"name": "Grace"})
    return f"<strong>{nested}</strong>"


result = await chevron.async_render(
    "{{#emphasize}}Hello {{name}}{{/emphasize}}",
    lambdas={"emphasize": emphasize},
)
# "<strong>Hello Grace</strong>"

The supplied helper retains the active rendering configuration and accepts optional temporary data. The recursion caused by application code calling this helper is application-owned; it uses the host Python call stack. Engine-owned expansion of partials and lambda results is iterative and has a finite safety bound.

docs.title: Cancellation and ownership
docs.text: Caller-owned readers and iterators remain open on success, error, and cancellation. Chevron closes only resources it opens for filesystem partials. The cleanup guarantee applies when cancellation is delivered by an AnyIO cancellation scope such as anyio.fail_after(), anyio.move_on_after(), or a task group's cancel_scope; raw asyncio cancellation APIs do not make the same guarantee.

docs.title: Diagnostics and logging
docs.text:
Chevron is quiet by default. Recoverable Mustache behaviour such as a missing partial renders an empty result without writing to the process log. Enable diagnostics only when an application wants them.

import logging
import chevron

logger = logging.getLogger("myapp.templates")
html = chevron.render(
    "{{> optional_banner}}<main>{{content}}</main>",
    {"content": "Ready"},
    logger=logger,
    log_level=logging.DEBUG,
)

Pass a standard-library logging.Logger or logging.LoggerAdapter through logger, with log_level as its paired minimum level. Chevron does not add handlers, change levels, or alter propagation; those remain application policy. Supplying logger (and its optional log_level) replaces warn; log_level alone does not enable diagnostics.

warn=True enables Chevron's historical default warning diagnostics. With a supplied logger, log_level=logging.INFO includes render lifecycle messages and logging.DEBUG adds bounded value-resolution and partial-selection decisions. Dynamic-partial diagnostics intentionally avoid recording the resolved selector value or template data.

Logging is synchronous in both APIs. Use the standard logging package's queue-based handlers if a destination could block; Chevron does not require a special async logger or wrapper.

docs.title: render()
docs.text:
chevron.render(template="", data={}, partials_path=None, partials_ext="mustache", partials_dict={}, padding="", def_ldel="{{", def_rdel="}}", scopes=None, warn=False, lambdas=None, *, logger=None, log_level=logging.WARNING)

render() returns the complete rendered string synchronously. It accepts template source text, a materialised token sequence, or an ordinary file-like object whose read() returns text. It does not close caller-owned readers.

import chevron

email = chevron.render(
    "Subject: {{subject}}\n\n{{> body}}",
    {"subject": "Build complete", "recipient": "Mina"},
    partials_dict={"body": "Hello {{recipient}}, your build is ready."},
)

docs.title: Inputs and configuration
docs.text:
data is the initial context. scopes supplies an existing sequence of contexts when an embedding application intentionally continues a render; ordinary callers should supply data instead. Chevron treats the outer scope sequence as private render state and does not mutate the caller's sequence.

def_ldel and def_rdel select initial delimiters. padding is an internal-compatible partial-indentation input and is rarely appropriate for application calls.

partials_dict is searched before partials_path. If filesystem partials are enabled, Chevron appends partials_ext (default mustache) and permits only resolved files contained by partials_path. An absolute partial name, parent traversal, unreadable file, or unavailable name renders as an empty partial and can be inspected through diagnostics.

lambdas selects explicit lambda mode; read Lambdas before exposing callbacks to template authors.

docs.title: Token streams
docs.text: Pass a materialised token sequence when template source has already been tokenized and validated. Do not pass the tokenize() generator directly if it must be reused: a generator is consumed after one render. The tokenizer API documents the accepted tuple shapes and structural validation.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Malformed template source raises chevron.ChevronError, a SyntaxError subclass. Direct-token structural errors also raise ChevronError, while malformed token values raise TypeError. An awaitable returned by a reader or lambda is rejected by render() with a TypeError that directs callers to async_render().

docs.title: chevron.tokenizer
docs.text:
The tokenizer is a supported submodule API for applications that inspect, cache, or transport template structure. Import it explicitly:

from chevron.tokenizer import tokenize

There is no chevron.tokenize root export.

import chevron
from chevron.tokenizer import tokenize

source = "{{#items}}<li>{{name}}</li>{{/items}}"
tokens = list(tokenize(source))

assert chevron.render(tokens, {"items": [{"name": "Ada"}]}) == "<li>Ada</li>"

tokenize() accepts source text only and returns a generator. Materialise it before caching or rendering more than once. render() and async_render() accept the materialised sequence and validate its structural nesting as they render it.

docs.title: Token shapes
docs.text:
By default every token is a two-item tuple: (tag_type, tag_key). include_raw=True emits three items: (tag_type, tag_key, raw_source). The raw stream retains source-only comment and standalone-whitespace records required by standard section lambdas.

tokens = list(tokenize("Hello {{name}}", include_raw=True))
# [("literal", "Hello ", "Hello "), ("variable", "name", "{{name}}")]

The renderer accepts a complete token sequence representing one whole template, not an arbitrary fragment to be spliced into an active render. It checks matching section, parent, and block boundaries. Structural errors raise chevron.ChevronError; malformed token values raise TypeError.

Tokenisation avoids repeating lexical work; it does not cache lookup, partial resolution, lambdas, or rendering. Applications that cache tokens therefore remain responsible for choosing an appropriate cache lifetime and for rerendering with current data.

docs.title: Template language overview
docs.text:
Mustache is deliberately small: tags look up values, sections select or repeat content, and partials compose templates. It is logic-light rather than logic-free; application code prepares meaningful data and templates render it predictably.

Read these chapters in order on a first pass:

  1. Values and contexts explains interpolation and lookup.
  2. Sections adds conditional and repeated output.
  3. Partials and layouts composes reusable fragments and inheritance layouts.
  4. Syntax and whitespace records delimiter and indentation rules that affect real files.
  5. Lambdas covers the narrowly defined extension points where application code participates in rendering.

Chevron's language target is the pinned upstream Mustache manual, not an independently invented dialect. Read Mustache and conformance when you need the authoritative upstream context or fixture provenance.

docs.title: Lambdas
docs.text:
Most templates need only data, sections, and partials. Lambdas are an explicit bridge to application code for cases such as localized fragments or a controlled transformation. They are not a general sandbox.

For new applications, pass a lambdas mapping. That enables only declared callable names and gives that mapping precedence over template data. lambdas={} disables callable tags altogether. Callable values found in ordinary template data are rejected in explicit mode.

docs.title: Interpolation and section lambdas
docs.text:
@chevron.func declares a zero-argument interpolation lambda. Its returned template source is rendered using the configured default delimiters:

@chevron.func
def banner() -> str:
    return "{{environment}} deployment"

@chevron.section declares a standard one-argument section lambda. It receives the literal section body and returns template source:

@chevron.section
def twice(body: str) -> str:
    return body + body

These definitions make the callable's intent visible. Both protocols may return awaitables under async_render(), but not under synchronous render().

docs.title: Compatibility callbacks
docs.text: @chevron.compat marks Chevron's historical two-argument section callback. It receives the literal body and a render helper. In synchronous rendering the helper is a normal callable. In async rendering it always returns an awaitable, even for a synchronous callback; read the async compatibility contract before using it.

docs.title: Partials and layouts
docs.text:
A partial, {{> card}}, renders another template with the active context. Supply reusable fragments through partials_dict when the application owns them in memory:

chevron.render(
    "{{#products}}{{> product_card}}{{/products}}",
    {"products": [{"name": "Keyboard"}, {"name": "Trackpad"}]},
    partials_dict={"product_card": "<article>{{name}}</article>\n"},
)

Filesystem lookup is disabled unless partials_path is supplied. Chevron rejects absolute names, parent traversal, and resolved paths outside that directory. Use a mapping when selection must be an allow-list; see render() for the partial lookup order.

docs.title: Dynamic names
docs.text:
{{>*selector}} resolves selector from the active context and uses its string value as the partial name. It is useful when data selects one of a known set of components:

{{#notifications}}
  {{>*presentation.partial}}
{{/notifications}}

With presentation.partial set to warning or success, the surrounding context remains available to the selected partial. A dynamic name still uses mapped-partial precedence and filesystem containment. Empty, non-string, missing, or doubly dereferenced names render nothing.

docs.title: Inheritance layouts
docs.text:
Parents provide named blocks; a child invocation replaces those blocks:

{{< page}}
  {{$title}}Release {{version}}{{/title}}
  {{$body}}{{> release_body}}{{/body}}
{{/page}}

The parent page might contain <title>{{$title}}Untitled{{/title}}</title> and <main>{{$body}}Empty{{/body}}</main>. The first block of a given name in the invoking template is the deterministic replacement. Parent names may also be dynamic with {{<*layout}}...{{/*layout}}.

*, <, and $ are meaningful tag prefixes. See compatibility before relying on literal partial names beginning with * or variables beginning with < or $.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
Sections use {{#name}}...{{/name}}. They are the main way to express optional and repeated content without placing conditional code in a template.

{{#release}}
## {{version}}
{{#changes}}- {{kind}}: {{summary}}
{{/changes}}
{{^changes}}- No user-facing changes.
{{/changes}}
{{/release}}

When release is a mapping, its fields become the nearest context for its body. When changes is a list, the body renders once per item; outer values such as version remain available. An empty list, false, or a missing value skips the ordinary section and selects the inverted section, {{^changes}}...{{/changes}}.

For a list of strings, {{.}} refers to each current item. For a boolean, a truthy value renders the body once without adding a new useful mapping context.

Sections are also the historical shape of Mustache lambdas. Chevron supports them deliberately, but they are application callbacks rather than template-defined functions; see lambdas.

docs.title: Syntax and whitespace
docs.text:
Mustache normally uses {{ and }}. Delimiters can change inside a template when embedding another language that uses braces:

{{=<% %>=}}
const release = "<% version %>";
<%={{ }}=%>
Published by {{author}}.

The delimiter change itself produces no output. render() and async_render() can also set the initial pair through def_ldel and def_rdel.

docs.title: Standalone lines and indentation
docs.text:
When a comment, section tag, partial, parent, block, or delimiter-change tag is alone on a line apart from spaces, Mustache removes that whole line. This lets structural tags stay readable without leaving blank lines in the output.

Indented partials apply their leading whitespace to every non-empty line produced by the partial. This is useful for YAML, configuration, and HTML fragments:

services:
  {{> worker}}

If worker contains image: app:1\nports: [8080], the output remains indented under services. The same rules apply when a partial participates in an inheritance layout; see partials and layouts.

docs.title: Values and contexts
docs.text:
{{name}} interpolates a value from the active context and HTML-escapes it. Use {{{name}}} or {{& name}} only when the application intentionally supplies already-safe markup.

<h2>{{project.name}}</h2>
<p>Requested by {{requester}}</p>
<div class="preview">{{{preview_html}}}</div>

With {"project": {"name": "Quarterly plan"}, "requester": "Ari & Co.", "preview_html": "<em>Draft</em>"}, this renders Ari & Co. in ordinary interpolation and retains the trusted <em> element only for the explicit unescaped tag.

docs.title: Lookup rules
docs.text:
Names can be dotted: {{project.name}} traverses mapping-like or attribute-based values. Chevron searches the current context first and then outer contexts, which is why a page-level value can remain visible within a section. {{.}} selects the current context itself, useful when iterating simple values.

Missing values render as an empty string. That makes optional display data straightforward, but an application should validate required business data before rendering rather than relying on an empty result.

Comments, {{! internal note }}, never appear in output. See syntax and whitespace for how a comment on its own line also removes that line's indentation and newline.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Chevron preserves the ordinary Mustache rendering model while documenting a few deliberate compatibility boundaries introduced by current conformance support.

docs.title: Names with reserved prefixes
docs.text:
* begins a dynamic partial or parent name. A literal partial whose name begins with * is therefore no longer available. Chevron 0.14.0 treated that form as a literal name. Names that use special tag-prefix characters are not a portable partial naming convention.

< begins a parent tag and $ begins a named block tag. Consequently, {{<name}} and {{$name}} are not interpolations of variables beginning with those characters; they must form matching parent or block structures.

docs.title: Existing lambda callbacks
docs.text: When lambdas is omitted, Chevron retains historical compatibility behavior for callable values found through template data. New applications should use an explicit mapping and decorators so their callable policy is visible. See Lambdas and the async_render() compatibility contract.

docs.title: Current-directory partial lookup
docs.text: The library API disables filesystem partial lookup by default. Passing partials_path="." deliberately restores the historical current-directory behavior. The command-line interface retains its established current-directory default; use --path to select a directory explicitly.

docs.title: Chevron extensions
docs.text: Chevron adds a small set of documented interfaces around Mustache rather than changing the ordinary value, section, and partial model.

docs.title: Explicit lambda protocols
docs.text: chevron.func, chevron.section, and chevron.compat make a callable's template role explicit. Passing a lambdas mapping enables explicit mode, where undeclared callable data is rejected and the mapping takes precedence. This is a Chevron API feature; see Lambdas.

docs.title: Async rendering
docs.text: async_render() integrates with a caller-owned AnyIO runtime. It awaits declared lambdas, async readers, and async iterables while preserving ordinary Mustache output semantics. It is an API extension, not an alternative template syntax; see async rendering.

docs.title: Safe filesystem partials
docs.text: Library filesystem partials are opt-in. partials_path confines resolved partial files to one directory and rejects absolute or escaping names. This is an application boundary, not a claim that rendering untrusted data is generally safe; see render().

docs.title: Direct token streams
docs.text: The chevron.tokenizer submodule exposes pre-parsing for applications that own template caching or inspection. It does not introduce a compiled-template format or change the template language. See the tokenizer API.

docs.title: Mustache and conformance
docs.text:
Chevron follows the upstream Mustache manual at commit 115baf2. That pinned revision is the normative language reference for tags, sections, partials, delimiter changes, lambdas, dynamic names, and inheritance.

The repository vendors the upstream specification fixtures under tests/fixtures/mustache-spec/. They are test inputs, not another user guide. Chevron marks them as conformance tests and records their upstream provenance in the fixture attribution.

The guide explains the practical subset an application developer needs to use Chevron successfully. When wording differs in level of detail, the upstream manual defines the language and Chevron's extensions and compatibility notes define the renderer-specific contract.
